sections.body_md:
Cauchy-Schwarz limits how large an inner product can be. For any vectors,
\[
\lvert\langle x, y \rangle\rvert \le \lVert x \rVert\,\lVert y \rVert,
\]
where the norm is the one induced by the inner product. The geometric reading is that the absolute cosine of an angle cannot exceed 1. The algebraic reading is that a square length cannot be negative.

Equality is informative. It holds when one vector is a scalar multiple of the other, including the case where either vector is zero. Orthogonal nonzero vectors do not give equality: their inner product is zero while the right-hand side is positive. So equality detects parallel vectors, not perpendicular ones.

The same bound proves the triangle inequality. Expand \(\lVert x+y \rVert^2\), replace the cross term by its Cauchy-Schwarz upper bound, and the right-hand side becomes \((\lVert x \rVert + \lVert y \rVert)^2\). Taking square roots gives \(\lVert x+y \rVert \le \lVert x \rVert + \lVert y \rVert\).

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
The inequality is \(\lvert\langle x,y \rangle\rvert \le \lVert x \rVert\,\lVert y \rVert\). One proof uses the quadratic
\[
q(t) = \lVert y \rVert^2\, t^2 + 2\langle x,y \rangle\, t + \lVert x \rVert^2 = \lVert x + t y \rVert^2 \ge 0.
\]
A quadratic that never goes negative has a nonpositive discriminant, and that discriminant condition is Cauchy-Schwarz. Equality holds when \(x\) and \(y\) are linearly dependent.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take \(x = (3,1)\) and \(y = (1,3)\). The inner product is 6. Each squared length is \(9+1 = 10\), so each length is \(\sqrt{10}\) and the product of the lengths is 10. Cauchy-Schwarz says the absolute inner product cannot exceed that product. Here the inner product 6 is strictly below the product 10, because neither vector is a multiple of the other.

The ratio \(6/10 = 0.6\) is the cosine of the angle. If \(y\) were replaced by \((6,2)\), a positive multiple of \(x\), the ratio would rise to 1 and equality would hold.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The inequality bounds the absolute value. A negative inner product is still fine, and the bound applies to its magnitude. Equality is not the orthogonal case. Dropping the absolute value and writing \(\langle x,y \rangle \le \lVert x \rVert\,\lVert y \rVert\) is true, but the matching lower bound needs the minus sign. The triangle inequality is a consequence, not a replacement: \(\lVert x+y \rVert\) can be strictly smaller than the sum of the lengths. Applying the result to a pairing that is not an inner product is not justified.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Each row of a matrix dotted with a vector is an inner product, so Cauchy-Schwarz bounds \(\lVert Ax \rVert_2\) by the Frobenius norm of \(A\) times \(\lVert x \rVert_2\). That comparison is the doorway to induced matrix norms. The 2-norm also defines the balls used for open sets. When a later convergence argument expands a squared norm and has to absorb a cross term, this inequality is the estimate it uses.
